title: Sugar, Olives and Galoshes: Vehbi Koç's Grocery in Ankara, 1917
dek: Taken out of school by a family short of money, sixteen-year-old Vehbi Koç opened a corner shop in Ankara with his father.

story.event: Leaving school and opening a small corner grocery in Ankara with his father, then widening it against his father's wishes
story.summary: In 1916 Vehbi Koç was withdrawn from school in Ankara at his grandfather's request, citing income difficulties, and in 1917, aged sixteen, he opened a small corner grocery with his father beneath the family houses. After Ankara became the capital in 1923 he widened it into hardware and building materials although his father opposed the idea, and on 31 May 1926 he registered the business in his own name with the Ankara Chamber of Commerce, the date from which the Koç Group counts its history.
paragraphs: In 1916 Vehbi Koç was in his last year of middle school at Ankara's high school, the Taş Mektep, and doing well; a 2018 Habertürk profile says he ranked first or second in his classes. That year, according to the Vehbi Koç Foundation's encyclopedia, his grandfather asked for him to be withdrawn, citing the family's "income difficulties", so that he could start working sooner. Ankara was then a provincial town of about 30,000 people in central Anatolia.

In 1917, at sixteen, he opened a corner shop with his father, Koçzade Hacı Mustafa Efendi, a literary scholar, in premises beneath the family's houses on Karaoğlan Caddesi. The company's history and a standard reference history of Koç Holding both say it was Vehbi who persuaded his father to do it. Habertürk puts the capital at 120 lira. The first stock was what a market town bought every week: rubber galoshes, sugar, olives, pasta and kaşar cheese, with herbs and spices.

Then the town changed around the shop. In 1923 the new republic made Ankara its capital, and building began. Vehbi widened the business into ironmongery, leather goods and construction materials, although, the foundation's encyclopedia says, his father opposed the idea; he later won a contract to replace the parliament's roof. In the first week of 1926 he married Sadberk Aktar, his father's business passed to him, and on 31 May 1926 he registered it with the Ankara Chamber of Commerce as Koçzade Ahmet Vehbi. In 1928, the year his father died, he took the Ankara agencies for Ford and Standard Oil.

The corner shop became the first step of the Koç Group, which marked its centenary in Ankara in June 2026, counting from that registration. In 1960, when his daughter Suna was about to go to the United States to study, he told her, as she later recalled, that his shop counter was the best university; she joined the family firm's Istanbul branch that October and worked beside him for about thirty-five years. His family also remembered a rule about money: he might fail to collect what others owed him, but his own debts he would pay to the last kuruş.

quote.text: As the bee collects nectar and departs without injuring the flower, or its colour or scent, so let a sage dwell in his village.
quote.source_title: Dhammapada, a Collection of Verses, tr. F. Max Müller, Project Gutenberg eBook #2017
quote.connection: The verse is about a monk begging in his village, not a trader, and a shop must take more than nectar. Yet the rule Koç's family remembered, paying his own debts to the last kuruş whatever others owed him, reads like a merchant's attempt at the bee's way: to live off a town without leaving it poorer.

reflection: Koç's start was not a bold leap from comfort. A grandfather worried about money took him out of school, and the first shop sat beneath the family's own houses, selling galoshes and olives to neighbours. The larger moves came later, when the town changed, and some of them he made against his father's advice.

You may also be building partly by choice and partly because circumstances pushed. Neither makes the work less yours. What stays in your hands, in a small place or a large one, is whether the people nearest to it are better off for it, and whether you are square with them.
invitation: Think of one person you owe something to at the moment, whether a reply, a small sum or a promised favour. Settle it today, before you start anything new.

cross_checks.claim: In 1917, aged sixteen, Vehbi Koç opened a small grocery in Ankara with his father.
He widened the business into hardware and construction materials as Ankara grew.
Koç registered the business with the Ankara Chamber of Commerce on 31 May 1926.
In 1928 Koç became the Ankara agent for Ford.

research_notes: Why he left school: Habertürk says he left despite his success, taking a certificate, to go into business; the Vehbi Koç Foundation Encyclopedia says his grandfather requested his withdrawal in 1916 on the grounds of income difficulties so that he could start work sooner. The two are compatible; the story gives the foundation's account with Habertürk's note on his grades. Who took the initiative: Koç Holding and the International Directory of Company Histories say Vehbi persuaded his father; the foundation says they opened the shop together; an Anadol fan-club page says the father opened it for him. The story follows the first three. Location: the foundation gives the family houses on Karaoğlan Caddesi and Habertürk the Karaoğlan market; the Turkish online encyclopedia Küre says Samanpazarı. The story follows the foundation. The 120 lira capital and the stock list come from Habertürk alone and are attributed to it. Expansion: Koç Holding ties the move into building materials and hardware to Ankara becoming the capital in 1923; the foundation (and Küre) say his father opposed the expansion. 1926: the foundation says the business passed to him after his marriage in the first week of 1926; Koç Holding says he registered the store in his own name; Habertürk says he took over his father's business; all agree on the 31 May 1926 registration at the Ankara Chamber of Commerce, which 2026 press reports also give. Ford and Standard Oil: the foundation and the reference history date the Ford agency to 1928; the reference history names Mobil where others say Standard Oil. Koç's memoir, Hayat Hikâyem, could not be read from a lawful online copy and is not cited directly; the 'shop counter' remark is paraphrased because the only source gives it in Turkish ('Benim tezgâhım en iyi üniversitedir'), and the debt maxim is likewise paraphrased from Hürriyet, whose piece was compiled from the Koç group's in-house magazine. Koç Holding's history page loads in a browser but returned an error to the checker; its claims are also supported by the foundation encyclopedia and the reference history. The Dhammapada verse is about a monk's alms round; the connection applies it to a shopkeeper by analogy.
